Discrete Weibull Distribution

Source: R/dweib.R
DiscreteWeibull.Rd

Density, distribution function, quantile function, and random generation for the (type I) discrete Weibull distribution of Nakagawa and Osaki (1975).

Usage

ddweib(x, theta, shape, log = FALSE)

pdweib(q, theta, shape, lower.tail = TRUE, log.p = FALSE)

qdweib(p, theta, shape, lower.tail = TRUE, log.p = FALSE)

rdweib(n, theta, shape)

Arguments

x

vector of (non-negative integer) quantiles.

theta

vector of values of the parameter \(\theta\), with \(0 < \theta < 1\). It equals \(P(Y \geq 1)\).

shape

vector of values of the shape parameter \(\beta > 0\).

log, log.p

logical; if TRUE, probabilities p are given as log(p).

q

vector of quantiles.

lower.tail

logical; if TRUE (default), probabilities are \(P(Y \leq y)\), otherwise \(P(Y > y)\).

p

vector of probabilities.

n

number of observations. If length(n) > 1, the length is taken to be the number required.

Value

ddweib gives the probability mass, pdweib the distribution function, qdweib the quantile function, and rdweib random deviates. The length of the result is determined by n for rdweib, and is the maximum of the lengths of the numerical arguments for the other functions (zero if any is zero).

Details

The discrete Weibull distribution has survival function $$P(Y \geq y) = \theta^{y^\beta}, \quad y = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$$ so that $$P(Y = y) = \theta^{y^\beta} - \theta^{(y+1)^\beta}, \qquad P(Y \leq y) = 1 - \theta^{(y+1)^\beta}.$$ It is the distribution of \(\lfloor X \rfloor\) where \(X\) has a continuous Weibull distribution with shape \(\beta\) and survival function \(\exp(-c x^\beta)\), \(c = -\log\theta\); rdweib() uses that representation. With \(\beta = 1\) it is the geometric distribution with success probability \(1 - \theta\) (dgeom(x, 1 - theta)).

The moments have no closed form: $$E[Y] = \sum_{k \geq 1} \theta^{k^\beta}, \qquad E[Y^2] = \sum_{k \geq 1} (2k - 1)\theta^{k^\beta}.$$ The distribution can be under- or overdispersed relative to the Poisson, which makes it a flexible model for counts (Klakattawi et al., 2018).

This is a discrete response distribution; it is unrelated to the Poisson-Weibull mixture of dpoisweibull.

All computations use the logarithms of the tail probabilities, so the upper tail lower.tail = FALSE keeps its relative accuracy far into the tail. qdweib() inverts the survival function exactly and returns the smallest \(y\) with \(P(Y \leq y) \geq p\).

Invalid parameter values give NaN with a warning, and non-integer x has probability 0 (with a warning), as in base R.

References

Nakagawa, T. and Osaki, S. (1975). The discrete Weibull distribution. IEEE Transactions on Reliability, R-24(5), 300-301.

Klakattawi, H., Vinciotti, V. and Yu, K. (2018). A simple and adaptive dispersion regression model for count data. Entropy, 20(2), 142.

Examples

ddweib(0:5, theta = 0.7, shape = 1.5)
#> [1] 0.30000000 0.33535430 0.20793242 0.09906527 0.03910657 0.01325193
# shape = 1 gives the geometric distribution
all.equal(ddweib(0:10, theta = 0.6, shape = 1), dgeom(0:10, prob = 0.4))
#> [1] TRUE
pdweib(3, theta = 0.7, shape = 1.5)
#> [1] 0.942352
pdweib(60, theta = 0.7, shape = 1.5, lower.tail = FALSE, log.p = TRUE)
#> [1] -169.9289
qdweib(c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9), theta = 0.7, shape = 1.5)
#> [1] 0 1 3
set.seed(1)
y <- rdweib(1000, theta = 0.9, shape = 0.8)
c(mean = mean(y), var = var(y))   # overdispersed
#>     mean      var 
#>  18.9820 549.8495
